quotes.text: “Never say of anything, "I have lost it," but, "I have restored it.".”
“No one can hurry me down to Hades before my time.”
“The happy life is thought to be virtuous; now a virtuous life requires exertion, and does not consist in amusement.”
“And if this is so, free-will must necessarily be very closely related to reason.”
quotes.attribution: John of Damascus  ·  Orthodox Faith II.27  [S26]
quotes.displayAttribution: John of Damascus · Orthodox Faith II.27

quotes.text: “The coward, then, is a despairing sort of person; for he fears everything.”
“What I write here I did not see myself, but I heard it told by men who were positive that they had seen it.”
“I know the height of God, and the weakness of man, and, on the contrary, his power.”
“If your opponent is of choleric temper, seek to irritate him.”
quotes.attribution: Sun Tzu  ·  Art of War I.22  [S45]
quotes.displayAttribution: Sun Tzu · Art of War I.22

quotes.text: “Do not disturb thyself by thinking of the whole of thy life.”
“Because of the cannon’s thick smoke, almost nothing could be seen.”
quotes.attribution: Nicolò Barbaro  ·  Siege Diary p. 54  [S35]  ·  Translation

quotes.text: “And bring not all the mischief you are able to do upon an enemy, for he may one day become your friend.”
“It is not necessary that the general be rich or poor; he may be the one or the other.”
“We demand, how much a man hath done; but from how much virtue he acted, is not so narrowly considered.”
quotes.attribution: Thomas à Kempis  ·  Imitation of Christ III.31  [S47]  ·  Literary voice
quotes.displayAttribution: Thomas à Kempis · Imitation of Christ III.31

quotes.text: “For the man who himself does no wrong is not just, unless he is also accustomed to rescue those who are wronged by others when he has it in his power.”
quotes.attribution: Lazic envoys in Procopius  ·  Wars II.15  [S41]  ·  Literary speech
quotes.displayAttribution: Lazic envoys in Procopius · Wars II.15

quotes.text: “Demand not that events should happen as you wish; but wish them to happen as they do happen, and you will go on well.”
“Attack him where he is unprepared, appear where you are not expected.”
quotes.attribution: Sun Tzu  ·  Art of War I.24  [S45]
quotes.displayAttribution: Sun Tzu · Art of War I.24

quotes.text: “For Christ is the sea, and He can receive — the fountains and brooks, the rivers and streams, that flow from the midst of the Scriptures.”
“For a hostile trumpet heard at night from the walls brings great terror to the besieged.”
“For that which is the result of compulsion has neither reason nor virtue in it.”
quotes.attribution: John of Damascus  ·  Orthodox Faith II.29  [S26]
quotes.displayAttribution: John of Damascus · Orthodox Faith II.29

quotes.text: “Without labour thou drawest not near to rest, nor without fighting comest thou to victory.”
quotes.attribution: Thomas à Kempis  ·  Imitation of Christ III.19  [S47]  ·  Literary voice
quotes.displayAttribution: Thomas à Kempis · Imitation of Christ III.19

quotes.text: “It is the men, the real swordsmen, who do whatever is done in battles.”
quotes.attribution: Xenophon in his Anabasis  ·  Anabasis III.2  [S50]  ·  Reported speech
quotes.displayAttribution: Xenophon in his Anabasis · Anabasis III.2

quotes.text: “Keep more reserves behind the line rather than spread your men too widely.”
“What the Emperor determines has the force of a statute.”
quotes.attribution: Justinian I and his jurists  ·  Institutes I.2.6  [S28]
quotes.displayAttribution: Justinian I and his jurists · Institutes I.2.6

quotes.text: “Therefore, Lucilius, do as you write me that you are doing: hold every hour in your grasp.”
“He must never shirk either blaming his friends or praising his enemies.”
“They only succeeded in creating hatred and wars among men, destroying the Law, and disuniting the people completely.”
“If you know the enemy and know yourself, you need not fear the result of a hundred battles.”
quotes.attribution: Sun Tzu  ·  Art of War III.18  [S45]
quotes.displayAttribution: Sun Tzu · Art of War III.18

quotes.text: “Whoever fails to prepare grain and necessities is defeated without a sword.”
“The aim of moral discipline is to purify the heart from the rust of passion and resentment, till, like a clear mirror, it reflects the light of God.”
“We considered ourselves secure against the Turkish fleet, especially with the chain across the harbour.”
quotes.attribution: Nicolò Barbaro  ·  Siege Diary p. 20  [S35]  ·  Translation

quotes.text: “While we are postponing, life speeds by.”
“There were two or three trumpeters on each galley; it sounded as though there were at least twenty galleys.”
quotes.attribution: Nicolò Barbaro  ·  Siege Diary p. 24  [S35]  ·  Translation

quotes.text: “Terror and dread alone are the weak bonds of attachment; which once broken, they who cease to fear will begin to hate.”
quotes.attribution: Calgacus in Tacitus  ·  Agricola 32  [S46]  ·  Literary speech

quotes.text: “Reason may be called the vizier, or prime minister, passion the revenue-collector, and anger the police-officer.”
“For men are able to learn from men more directly about higher things.”
quotes.attribution: Athanasius of Alexandria  ·  On the Incarnation 12.2  [S07]
quotes.displayAttribution: Athanasius of Alexandria · On the Incarnation 12.2

quotes.text: “When you learn that your plan has been betrayed, change your dispositions.”
“But if such restraint is not easy, we shall at least curb our anger by reflection, so as not to give it too much rein.”
quotes.attribution: Basil of Caesarea  ·  To Young Men VII  [S09]
quotes.displayAttribution: Basil of Caesarea · To Young Men VII

quotes.text: “Never lead a soldier into battle before you have tested him.”

sources.title: Abba Moses in John Cassian  Conferences
sources.notes: Written c. 426. E. C. S. Gibson, Nicene and Post Nicene Fathers, second series XI, 1894; conference I. Abba Moses is the literary speaker.

sources.title: Aeneas Tacticus  Siege Defence
sources.notes: Written mid fourth century BC. Illinois Greek Club, Loeb, 1923/1928.

sources.title: Al-Ghazali  Alchemy of Happiness
sources.notes: Written c. 1100. Claud Field, 1909, translated through Hindustani; chapters I and VI.

sources.title: Anna Komnene  Alexiad
sources.notes: Written c. 1148. Elizabeth A. S. Dawes, 1928. Page references follow the bracketed original page numbers in the Fordham text.

sources.title: Aphrahat  Demonstration 8
sources.notes: Written 337. John Gwynn, Nicene and Post Nicene Fathers, second series XIII, 1898. Demonstration on the resurrection.

sources.title: Aristotle  Nicomachean Ethics
sources.notes: Written fourth century BC. W. D. Ross, 1925, books II, III and X, cited by chapter.

sources.title: Athanasius of Alexandria  On the Incarnation
sources.notes: Written fourth century. Archibald Robertson, Nicene and Post Nicene Fathers, second series IV, 1892.

sources.title: Augustine of Hippo  Confessions
sources.notes: Written c. 397–400. E. B. Pusey, 1838; Gutenberg 3296. Citations use book, chapter and paragraph.

sources.title: Basil of Caesarea  To Young Men
sources.notes: Written c. 370. F. M. Padelford, Essays on the Study and Use of Poetry, 1902, pp. 101–120.

sources.title: Boethius  Consolation
sources.notes: Written c. 524. H. R. James, 1897. Philosophy is a literary personification; her words are not a report of a historical conversation.

sources.title: Cicero  On Duties
sources.notes: Written 44 BC. Walter Miller, Loeb, 1913; Gutenberg 47001. Book and numbered section references.

sources.title: Dante Alighieri  Inferno
sources.notes: Written c. 1308–1321. Henry Wadsworth Longfellow, 1867. Verse numbers follow the Italian text. Quotations are literary dialogue or inscriptions, not historical reported speech.

sources.title: Ephrem the Syrian  Epiphany Hymns
sources.notes: Written Syriac Ephrem tradition, fourth century and later. J. B. Morris and A. E. Johnston, Nicene and Post Nicene Fathers, second series XIII, 1898. Hymns transmitted under Ephrem’s name; individual attribution is not uniformly certain.

sources.title: Epictetus via Arrian  Enchiridion
sources.notes: Written c. 125. Thomas Wentworth Higginson’s nineteenth century translation, reprinted in the Liberal Arts Press edition, 1955; Gutenberg 45109. The modern introduction by Albert Salomon is not used.

sources.title: Frontinus  Stratagems
sources.notes: Written first century AD or later ancient compilation. Charles E. Bennett, Loeb, 1925; book IV is transmitted with the work but its authorship has been questioned. Reported sayings are anecdotal.

sources.title: George Sphrantzes  Chronicle Minor
sources.notes: Written c. 1470s. Marios Philippides, The Fall of the Byzantine Empire, 1980; §§35–36 excerpted by De Re Militari. Authentic short chronicle, not the sixteenth century Chronicle Major.

sources.title: Gregory Palamas  150 Chapters
sources.notes: Written c. 1349–1350. Robert E. Sinkewicz, The One Hundred and Fifty Chapters, 1988, Greek and English reproduced at Azbyka. CP entries are short editorial paraphrases, not verbatim Sinkewicz quotations.

sources.title: Gregory of Nazianzus  Oration 2
sources.notes: Written 362. C. G. Browne and J. E. Swallow, Nicene and Post Nicene Fathers, second series VII, 1894.

sources.title: Herodotus  Histories
sources.notes: Written fifth century BC. G. C. Macaulay, 1890, volume I; Gutenberg 2707. Speeches and anecdotes are the historian’s reports.

sources.title: Homer  Iliad
sources.notes: Written eighth or seventh century BC. Samuel Butler, 1898; Gutenberg 2199. Book references suffice for these short prose excerpts; all speakers are epic characters.

sources.title: Homer  Odyssey
sources.notes: Written eighth or seventh century BC. Samuel Butler, 1900; Gutenberg 1727. Epic literary dialogue.

sources.title: Ibn Khaldun  Muqaddimah
sources.notes: Written 1377; later revisions. Franz Rosenthal, 1958, chapter III §§12 and 41. One brief verbatim excerpt; the other entries are labelled close paraphrases.

sources.title: Ibn Rushd  Decisive Discourse
sources.notes: Written c. 1179–1180. Mohammad Jamil-ur-Rehman, The Philosophy and Theology of Averroes, 1921. Locations refer to the short treatise or its stated argument, rather than modern paragraph numbers.

sources.title: Jalal al-Din Rumi  Masnavi
sources.notes: Written thirteenth century. James W. Redhouse, The Mesnevi, 1881, book I. “Proem” and couplet numbers follow Redhouse, whose numbering differs from Nicholson. The opening flute is a literary speaker.

sources.title: John Chrysostom  Matthew Homilies
sources.notes: Written c. 390. George Prevost, revised by M. B. Riddle, Nicene and Post Nicene Fathers, first series X, 1888. Homily 50.

sources.title: John of Damascus  Orthodox Faith
sources.notes: Written eighth century. S. D. F. Salmond, Nicene and Post Nicene Fathers, second series IX, 1899; book II.

sources.title: Julian  Letters
sources.notes: Written 362. Wilmer Cave Wright, Loeb, 1923; letters 22 to Arsacius and 37 to Atarbius. “Atheism” and “Galilaeans” here mean Christianity and Christians.

sources.title: Justinian I and his jurists  Institutes
sources.notes: Written 533. J. B. Moyle, fifth edition, 1913. Promulgated under Justinian; compiled by Tribonian, Theophilus and Dorotheus, drawing on earlier jurists.

sources.title: Kritoboulos of Imbros  History of Mehmed
sources.notes: Written 1460s. Charles T. Riggs, 1954, book I §§117–257, reproduced by De Re Militari. Contemporary Ottoman subject; not an eyewitness inside the besieged city. CP means editorial paraphrase; speeches are literary reconstructions.

sources.title: Loukas Notaras in Doukas  History
sources.notes: Written recorded c. 1462. Doukas, History 37.10, Greek quoted in A. Karpozilos, Byzantine Historians, pp. 270–288. Fresh translation. Doukas attributes the saying; it is not a verified verbatim utterance.

sources.title: Manuel II Palaiologos  Dialogues with a Persian
sources.notes: Written c. 1394–1402. Dialogue VII 2c, quoted from Théodore Khoury’s edition, 1966, pp. 144–145, in the Vatican transcript of 12 September 2006, note 4. The emperor’s literary dialogue, not a transcript of an exchange.

sources.title: Marcus Aurelius  Meditations
sources.notes: Written c. 170–180. George Long, 1862; Gutenberg 15877. Only Marcus’s numbered text is used, not Long’s essays.

sources.title: Michael Psellos  Chronographia
sources.notes: Written c. 1060s–1070s. E. R. A. Sewter, 1953, book I. Short editorial paraphrases of the cited passages, not verbatim Sewter translations.

sources.title: Moses Maimonides  Guide for the Perplexed
sources.notes: Written c. 1190. Michael Friedländer, revised second edition, 1904, reprint 1910; Gutenberg 73584.

sources.title: Nicolò Barbaro  Siege Diary
sources.notes: Written 1453; later revision. Venetian text edited by Enrico Cornet, Giornale dell’assedio di Costantinopoli 1453, Vienna, 1856. Fresh English translation. Eyewitness diary revised after the event.

sources.title: Niketas Choniates  History
sources.notes: Written early thirteenth century. Dana C. Munro, The Fourth Crusade, 1896/revised 1912, pp. 15–16, from the narrative of the sack of 1204.

sources.title: Onasander  The General
sources.notes: Written first century AD. Illinois Greek Club, Loeb, 1923/1928.

sources.title: Plutarch  Parallel Lives
sources.notes: Written early second century AD. John Dryden translation revised by Arthur Hugh Clough, nineteenth century; Gutenberg 674. Reported sayings remain biographical anecdotes.

sources.title: Polybius  Histories
sources.notes: Written second century BC. W. R. Paton, Loeb, 1922; book I.

sources.title: Procopius  Secret History
sources.notes: Written c. 550. Anonymous English translation, 1896, Gutenberg 12916. A hostile polemic against Justinian and Theodora; its accusations remain the author’s claims.

sources.title: Procopius  Wars
sources.notes: Written c. 550. H. B. Dewing, 1914; books I and II, also called the Persian War. Speeches are historical compositions, not transcripts.

sources.title: Saadi  Gulistan
sources.notes: Written 1258. James Ross translation, in Persian Literature, revised edition II, 1900. Citations follow that edition’s chapter and story numbering.

sources.title: Seneca  Letters
sources.notes: Written c. 63–65. Richard M. Gummere, Moral Epistles, Loeb, 1917–1925.

sources.title: Socrates in Plato  Apology
sources.notes: Written fourth century BC. Benjamin Jowett, nineteenth century. Plato’s literary presentation of Socrates’s defence, not a stenographic transcript.

sources.title: Sun Tzu  Art of War
sources.notes: Written traditionally fifth century BC. Lionel Giles, 1910. Only the numbered ancient text is excerpted; Giles and later Chinese commentators are excluded.

sources.title: Tacitus  Agricola
sources.notes: Written c. 98. The Oxford Translation Revised, with an introduction by Edward Brooks Jr., 1897; Gutenberg 7524. Calgacus’s and Agricola’s speeches are literary compositions.

sources.title: Thomas à Kempis  Imitation of Christ
sources.notes: Written c. 1420–1441. William Benham, 1886; Gutenberg 1653. The book’s dialogue voices are literary devotional voices.

sources.title: Thucydides  Peloponnesian War
sources.notes: Written late fifth century BC. Richard Crawley, 1874. Book and section numbers are those of the Greek text; the speeches are the historian’s literary reconstructions.

sources.title: Vegetius  Military Epitome
sources.notes: Written late fourth or early fifth century. Latin text at The Latin Library, book III; fresh English translations.

sources.title: Xenophon  Anabasis
sources.notes: Written fourth century BC. H. G. Dakyns, 1897; Gutenberg 1170. Book and chapter references. Speeches are the author’s narrative reconstruction.
